author: .just_kk
content:
Posted fast proof broadcast protocol (framed it as an EIP in the write up)

https://notes.ethereum.org/@kamilsa/rk_I4TMJme

TLDR It is based on the 8411 with waggle ([link](https://github.com/ethereum/EIPs/pull/12671/changes)) : proof is chunked and then merkle tree is built on top. Root is signed by leanXMSS. Chunk size is ~3KB, signature size is 2.4KB, so we send signature only with the first chunk to the remote peer

Also vibed a Lighthouse branch on top of the pq-devnet-0 branch: https://github.com/kamilsa/lighthouse/tree/leanvm-proof-broadcast

author: kevaundray
content:
I believe this is within expectation! 

I'd say that the proof size is not directly related to the number of votes that the proof covers, but to the amount of work it took to make the proof.

Lets say "amount of work" is equal to the number of instructions.

I will use example numbers to make it easy for me to do the math.

- verifying an XMSS signature is 10 instructions
- verifying a stark proof is 123 instructions

Now lets say that 1 instruction adds 3B to the proof size.

**Case 1a:** I want to aggregate 200 XMSS signatures

This maps to verifying 200 XMSS signatures so the proof size is 200 * 10 * 3 = 6KB

**Case 1b: **I want to aggregate 400 XMSS signatures

This maps to verifying 400 XMSS signatures so the proof size is 400 * 10 * 3 = 12KB

I think at this point, the idea of more signatures means a bigger proof makes sense, and its what usually happens when we verify signatures in a committee.

**Case 2:** I want to aggregate 400 XMSS signatures, then I want to aggregate one additional signature

Aggregating the first 400 XMSS signatures will give us a 12KB stark proof. However, when we add an additional signature we are actually verifying the existing stark proof and then verifying an XMSS signature. This is different to verifying 401 signatures in one go like the previous cases.

So the proof size would be (123 + 10) * 3 = 399 bytes

author: t.wambsgans
content: It's due to a technical reason, an optimization leanVM uses in WHIR (the polynomial commitment scheme), where some parts of the Merkle leaves (containing zeros) are omitted in the proof ("pruned leaves"). Committing to 25 variables where the polynomial is fully utilised, ends up being bigger than a half-used polynomial at 26 variables.
